title: ‘Paro: The Untold Story of Bride Slavery’ Explores the Plight of Women Caught in the Web of Bride Trafficking
subtitle: Actor-Producer and Screenplay writer Trupti Bhoir brings a hard-hitting story of exploitation, gender inequality and women’s rights to the 57th IFFI
body_text:
Posted On: 27 NOV 2026 4:15PM by PIB Mumbai Release ID: 2342558 Views: 36 A A Print Share X Facebook Instagram WhatsApp Copy Article Link
Read in: English
Goa, 27 November 2026 Paro: The Untold Story of Bride Slavery , featured in the Indian Panorama section of the 57 th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), brings to light the disturbing and largely under-reported practice of buying and selling women as brides, particularly in Mewat, Haryana. The term ‘Paro’ is used in the region to refer to women who are bought or sold into marriage. Speaking in a press conference, actor and producer Trupti Bhoir shared that, she has undertaken 4.5 years of research to make this film, which is her second Oscar-listed film. In an unusual creative journey in this film, Trupti Bhoir has taken on the triple responsibility of producer, screenplay writer and protagonist. A challenging research that led to making of the film The idea for the film emerged from Trupti Bhoir’s exposure to documentaries and media reports highlighting the practice of bride slavery in India. Known for films centred on women’s issues and rights, she was deeply disturbed by the realities she encountered. With the help of an NGO, Bhoir and her mother visited the villages disguised as journalists. They met around 62–63 women subjected to bride slavery, hailing from Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Gujarat and Delhi. Bhoir remarked that the bride trade is rooted in gender inequality and poverty. It is not confined to Haryana but is a wider national concern, with women and girls from several states falling victim to the practice. One of the most disturbing accounts uncovered during the research was that of a girl aged approximately 11–13 years, who had reportedly been sold for a meager amount. This young girl's story became the inspiration for the protagonist of the film, a character portrayed by Trupti Bhoir herself. Through this character, the filmmaker seeks to bring to the screen the pain, helplessness and brutal exploitation experienced by countless women whose stories often remain unheard. Taking the fight beyond cinema The film's significance extends beyond storytelling. Trupti Bhoir said that NGO Shelter Foundation has compiled data on approximately 2,000 women who are victims of bride slavery. The data was submitted to the Chairperson of the National Commission for Women, Vijaya Rahatkar, around a year and three months ago. A fact-finding committee has subsequently been constituted by the Union Government. “I salute the Government which has taken steps to address this issue. This is another reason for me to make this film,” she said. Trafficking of women: A global issue Bhoir also pointed out that missing girls and sexual violence are concerns across the world. While awareness about human trafficking and prostitution has increased significantly over the last 15–20 years, the buying and selling of brides and the practice of bride slavery continue to receive comparatively little attention. Her interactions during screenings at film festivals and institutions across the world have reinforced her belief that this issue needs greater international awareness and discussion. With ‘ Paro: The Untold Story of Bride Slavery ’, Trupti Bhoir hopes to take a deeply disturbing social issue from the margins to the mainstream and initiate conversations about gender inequality, bride slavery and the dignity and rights of women. The press conference was moderated by Shubhankar Vashisth.
